Patch change: >- req.query.name enters the /hello handler and is assigned to name. Originally, it was concatenated directly into an HTML response. The candidate adds a local escapeHtml function that converts the value to a string and encodes &, <, >, double quotes, single quotes, and backticks before res.send. The route still returns an

Hello [name]

greeting. Its wire-format changes for special characters, but the browser-visible text is preserved. The patch assumes name is plain text rather than intentionally supplied HTML, and that the escaped value remains in HTML element-content context. String(undefined) also preserves the original missing-name result, "undefined". Security observations: >- All four requests returned 200. The script-tag payload was returned as <script>...; the img/onerror payload had its markup delimiters encoded; the quote-plus-SVG payload encoded both the quote and markup delimiters; and the consecutive-markup payload encoded every relevant < and >. In every case, the raw response contained no executable version of the supplied markup and headless Chromium reported no dialogs or payload execution. These tests establish protection against the four tested reflected-XSS forms in the current HTML element-content sink, but they are a fixed payload suite rather than a general proof for every input or future output context. Functional observations: >- Tony and Tony Tran were returned unchanged. Inputs containing &, <, adjacent &<>, and "> were entity-encoded in the HTTP body but decoded to exactly the original browser-visible value. That expected behavior makes sense for a greeting route where a name is text, not markup. The tests therefore show that the patch does not strip or corrupt the tested special characters while neutralizing their HTML syntax. Why the SAST warning may persist: >- Both CWE-79 rules now point to candidate line 17, where res.send receives "

Hello " + escapeHtml(name) + "

". One rule conservatively detects user data in manually constructed HTML, and the other detects user input written directly to a response. Neither appears to recognize the custom escapeHtml helper as a trusted, context-appropriate sanitizer. Because the warning is located at the post-escaping sink, while code inspection and both response and browser evidence show effective encoding, the persistence most likely reflects a scanner modeling limitation rather than an ineffective repair. Remaining uncertainty or additional test needed: >- The existing suite does not cover empty or omitted name values, repeated query parameters, Unicode, entity-looking input such as <script>, single quotes, or backticks. It also detects execution primarily through alert dialogs. An optional stronger supplemental test would exercise those values and assert that the resulting h1 contains only one text node, has no attacker-created child elements, and displays the original input exactly. A property/fuzz test over arbitrary strings would provide broader assurance. This uncertainty does not reveal a concrete bypass in the present sink, because the implementation encodes ampersands before encoding every < delimiter. Proposed verdict and justification: >- ACCEPT_CANDIDATE within the controlled /hello-route scope. The patch applies correct HTML element-content encoding before the only response sink, preserves the route's intended visible greeting for the tested normal and special inputs, introduces no new SAST findings, and retains the original missing-name coercion behavior. The persistent scanner finding is best explained by lack of recognition of the local escaping helper. Acceptance would not imply that the helper is safe if its output is later reused in an attribute, URL, JavaScript, CSS, or another context.

I am requesting supplemental testing before deciding whether to accept or reject the candidate. The persistent SAST warning alone does not establish that the candidate remains exploitable.

I reviewed the candidate patch, automated primary decision, and all eight supplemental outcomes for this candidate. The patch replaces SQL string concatenation with a parameterized query. The primary target SAST finding resolved, and the candidate passed the original security and functional checks. In the supplement, it passed all three registered SQL-injection security cases, both behavioral-parity cases, and two of three robustness cases. SQL-R01 supplied repeated username parameters and returned HTTP 200 with an empty array instead of the registered HTTP 400 JSON error, so that robustness result remains failed. The response returned no user row and did not broaden the query result. Under my bounded criterion, this client-visible status-code difference is not severe enough to reject the tested SQL-injection repair. I accept the candidate for the bounded benchmark while explicitly retaining the SQL-R01 limitation. This is not full supplemental conformance or production approval, and it does not alter the primary record or metrics.

I reviewed the frozen PATH-S06 protocol, baseline gate, saved candidate, prior decisions, and registered extension result. The vulnerable baseline established the control by disclosing the outside-file marker through an in-root symbolic link. Traversal 01 then returned HTTP 200 and disclosed the same marker because its lexical path containment check did not verify the filesystem target followed by fs.readFile. I reaffirm FOLLOW_UP_REJECT_CANDIDATE for the bounded benchmark because the registered symbolic-link traversal remains exploitable. The earlier rejection and its separate parity and robustness findings remain preserved; this later qualification does not overwrite primary-v1 or supplemental-v1.

Additional testing needed: The candidate resolves the configured file root and requested path, computes the relative path, and rejects missing, absolute, or parent-relative paths. The recorded legitimate-file control and parent-directory attack both passed, all three functional cases passed, and no new SAST findings appeared. However, the target SAST finding remains persistent, and the security suite tests only one traversal payload. The condition rel.startsWith("..") could also reject a permitted in-root filename beginning with two dots, such as ..notes.txt, although this was not demonstrated by the frozen fixtures. Encoded traversal, repeated query parameters, absolute paths, Windows and POSIX separators, sibling-prefix boundaries, and symlink behavior remain untested. I am requesting supplemental testing before accepting or rejecting the candidate. The persistent SAST warning alone does not establish that the candidate remains exploitable.

I reviewed the candidate patch, original review, and all eleven supplemental traversal results. The candidate passed all five executable security cases, while PATH-S06 remained inconclusive because Windows could not create the required symlink fixture. PATH-P01 confirmed that the candidate rejects the valid in-root filename "..notes.txt", and PATH-R03 returned HTTP 404 rather than the predefined HTTP 400 response for repeated filenames. These results demonstrate a behavioral-parity failure and a robustness-contract failure. I reject the candidate for the bounded benchmark while preserving the symlink result as inconclusive.

I reviewed the frozen PATH-S06 protocol, baseline gate, saved candidate, prior decisions, and registered extension result, and I manually reproduced Traversal 02 in WSL2. The candidate preserved normal access to welcome.txt and returned HTTP 400 for a direct ../../ traversal request. However, an in-root symbolic link pointing outside the allowed directory bypassed the lexical path.resolve check. The candidate returned HTTP 200 and disclosed the controlled outside-file marker. I therefore record FOLLOW_UP_REJECT_CANDIDATE for the bounded benchmark because the registered PATH-S06 symbolic-link traversal remains exploitable. The earlier request-more-testing record remains preserved; this later qualification does not overwrite primary-v1 or supplemental-v1.

ACCEPT-CANDIDATE: The candidate requires the file name to be a nonempty string, resolves the configured root and requested path, and permits the read only when the resolved path equals the root or begins with the root plus the platform path separator. Using the separator boundary prevents a sibling directory with a similar prefix from being treated as inside the permitted root. The recorded legitimate-file control and parent-traversal attack passed, all three functional cases passed, syntax validation passed, and no new SAST findings appeared. The persistent CWE-22 warnings point to user input entering path.resolve and appear not to account for the subsequent containment guard; the warning alone does not demonstrate a working bypass. I accept the candidate within the controlled /file benchmark scope. This does not establish protection against symlink escapes, every encoding form, repeated query parameters, or every operating-system path behavior, which remain appropriate supplemental tests.

I reviewed the candidate patch, original acceptance, and all eleven supplemental traversal outcomes. The candidate passed both behavioral-parity cases, all three robustness cases, and all five executable security cases. PATH-S06 remains inconclusive because the Windows environment could not create the required symlink or junction fixture. The patch enforces a lexical resolved-root boundary, but the saved evidence does not establish containment of a filesystem target reached through an in-root link. I therefore request more testing in a symlink-capable environment rather than claiming complete traversal protection. This later conclusion preserves the original bounded acceptance, the inconclusive result, and all primary metrics.
